sections.section: Phase 0: Setup (working agreement, safety, confidentiality, Prime Directive)
rows: Read Norm Kerth's Retrospective Prime Directive aloud
At every retro: *"Regardless of what we discover, we understand and truly believe that everyone did the best job they could..."* — especially when blame language is anticipated.
Choose Vegas Rule or Chatham House Rule explicitly
A retro is about to start without a named confidentiality rule. Vegas Rule (unanimous explicit consent before sharing) or Chatham House Rule (information shared, identities not). Pick one.
Frame Vegas-rules privacy for online retros
Online-retro-specific privacy and confidentiality framing; recording-as-consent (not default).
Run a safety check at the start
Check-ins and Establish Shared Principles are the Open Practice Library practices for the safety move; if safety is 1-2, address it before the topic (the retro task spec rule, not the library's).
Establish shared principles before content
Against copy-practice-without-principles: copying practices without the values and principles behind them will not get the same result; name why and how the team will act before what it will do.
Handle a manager on the call

Field Guide strict participant control: no one else attends unless invited by the entire Scrum Team, and non-team attendees support rather than steer; FLO engagement-equity tracking matrix supports operationalising it.
Surface power-dynamics before opening
Engagement-equity tracking matrix; foundation-of-trust for honest exchange.
Set the Scrum Retrospective frame

Sprint Retrospective as one of the four inspect-and-adapt events inside the Sprint, the one that concludes it; team inspects individuals, interactions, processes, tools, Definition of Done; 3h timebox for monthly Sprint.
Default to the Derby-Larsen six-segment shape
The 1½-hour Sprint Retrospective in its six-segment form is the default; sample agenda concrete enough to facilitate.
Frame the retro as team-internal iterative, not incident-triggered
If the team is mid-incident, route to [[aar]] axis instead; retro is iterative team-internal cadence.
Hold default-to-system framing in the substrate
"Action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate" — even in retro context, the guide's prior, applied by analogy, frames blame language.
Read the team's Tuckman stage before opening

Forming (polite, surface), storming (contested), norming (ground rules), performing (self-directed): ask how much structure the stage calls for; with a storming team, acknowledge the storm before data gathering. Match the setup structure to the stage.
Check for hygiene-factor suppression before content

If a live anxiety (job security, org change, manager conflict) is in the room, Herzberg's hygiene framing suggests it may crowd out motivator-level engagement. Name it or address it before the topic phase.
Safety check returns 1-2

Ch 3 critique rule: a team member's willingness to admit mistakes "depends on the commander's willingness to tolerate them". Before asking for mistakes, the lead (and any manager) states that admitted mistakes will be discussed, not punished; trust "is a product of confidence and familiarity" and is not rebuilt in one retro.
Lead names manager on call

Brief the manager before the retro: open by stating tolerance for admitted mistakes (Ch 3, "Training"), and invite disagreement before the team commits; MCDP 1 makes honest opinion before a decision a duty (Ch 3, "Professionalism").
Hold a senior voice back until others have written
Lead names manager on call: pilot/co-pilot deference, the reluctance to challenge a senior person's opinions or decisions; have everyone write first and the senior speak last.

sections.section: Phase 0.5: Experiment review (what did we say last time, what happened)
rows: Review last retro's experiments without punishment
*Real benefits come from applying results* scales down to retro level; if the experiment was unowned, the experiment design failed, not the team.
Treat experiments as designed-not-declared
Design of Experiments practice — the experiment is a hypothesis, the outcome is the evidence.
Reframe locus-of-control when last experiment stalled
15% Solutions: *"Where do you have freedom to act? What's in your 15%?"* — the handbook's own question; it separately quotes Gareth Morgan on "15-percent initiatives", borrowed-through.
Detect *same experiment 3+ retros running* pattern
Fixes that fail or shifting the burden may be in play; surface as hypothesis-generator, not label.
Escalate when experiment crosses to structural-change

Holistic / Systemic value (Deming + Goldratt borrowed-through): "no single part of a system can ever bring overall improvement"; the team's part alone will not bring it, so raise fixes that lie outside the team rather than retry at team level.
Surface the *team is allergic to "experiments" framing* problem
Establish Shared Principles to surface why the word lands wrong before swapping vocabulary.
Detect the structural-repeat pattern when the same experiment re-surfaces

Third or fourth retro proposing essentially the same experiment is the structural-mismatch detection signal; ask whether the team is failing or retrospecting against a structural constraint it cannot change unilaterally.
Reframe from team-failure to structural-constraint

When an experiment hasn't taken hold, apply the Primer's single-team-island warning: "A single high-performing team can't deliver its full potential if surrounding structures and processes remain unchanged." Reframe before generating another 15% experiment.
Last retro's experiments weren't done

Sort before judging: an experiment tried boldly that failed is the kind of error MCDP 1 treats leniently (no "zero defects" mentality); one never started is inaction, taken up as a topic rather than a sanction. Ask why, starting with its owner and stated purpose (Ch 3, "Professionalism"; Ch 4, "Commander's intent").
Same experiment proposed three retros running

Main-effort rule: a commitment is "not an irretrievable one", and when shifting "we seek to exploit success rather than reinforce failure" (Ch 4, "Main effort"); ask what in this Sprint calls for the experiment, not habit (Ch 4, "Decisionmaking").
Check what the last experiments visibly changed

Last retro's experiments weren't done, or the same one is proposed again: people must see change in response to their feedback; latent conditions accumulate rather than fade, so a returning delta points at a condition present each time.

sections.section: Phase 1: Priming (set the topic frame, surface energy, choose retro shape)
rows: Choose the retro shape that fits this Sprint's content
Field Guide six-segment Derby-Larsen pattern is the default; sample agenda includes positives / deltas / insights / √n voting.
Reach for alternate retro shapes from the catalogue
Open Practice Library Retrospective practice with multiple shapes when the default doesn't fit.
Open with an energising structure
LS Impromptu Speed Networking or Knee-to-Knee Conversation as opener when team is low-energy.
Calibrate facilitator presence to phase
High-presence community building early; lighter once the team owns the conversation: participate in discussions but don't lead.
Frame AI-adoption-friction retro

Evals practice (against AI overconfidence); Human-in-the-Loop (against silent AI delegation); Establish Shared Principles to surface what principles govern the team's AI use before it commits to adoption or delegation.
Detect the *Anxious-Annie* facilitator pattern in oneself

When the urge to fill a silence or rush in because the stickies are sparse is rising — locate it as one's own anxiety, not the team's problem; let the silence breathe before prompting. *Trust the process*.
Route mid-incident to AAR axis
If the team is mid-incident rather than mid-iteration, retro is wrong axis; route to AAR.
Frame the retro through Scrum's empiricism pillars
Transparency / Inspection / Adaptation — the retro is where the team adapts its own way of working, one of the four inspect-and-adapt events inside the Sprint.
Use OT mapping as a priming activity when structural recurring topic is suspected

When the same topic has surfaced two or more retros with experiments not moving the needle, spend 10 minutes mapping the team's current archetype against the work being demanded. The mismatch (if any) is the priming insight that frames the data-gathering phase.
Surface the team's current archetype before content

Ask: what is our archetype today (TASKS-2 multi-skill incomplete? CAPS-2 multi-skill capability-focused? CAPS-3 end-to-end ownership)? What archetype does the work being demanded require? The gap, if named, changes the data-gathering frame.
Run chat-waterfall written-first input

Each team member writes positives / deltas / insights individually on stickies; group like items; vote on top 3 to deep-dive. (Applied reading: writing before talking keeps the first voice from setting the field.)
Run 1-2-4-All to refuse HiPPO-driven discussion

LS 1-2-4-All: individual reflection → pairs → groups of 4-6 → whole group; by the whole-group round every participant has formed and tested a view, so a dominant voice finds it harder to anchor the room.
Run 1-2-4-All from the Open Practice Library
Open Practice Library's 1-2-4-All practice — against HiPPOs.
Run Troika Consulting when team has parallel individual challenges
Three-person 10-min-per-focal-person rounds; peer honing → between-peer conversation → with-focal-person conversation.
Track engagement equity in real time

Contribution log adapted from FLO's engagement-equity tracking matrix (which logs the facilitator's own responses); surface who has spoken / not spoken; rebalance via written-first or structured rounds.
Surface artificial-harmony pattern when team agrees too quickly
LS Mini Constellations: spatial positioning by degree of agreement; speak from the distance as a "role"; surfaces range without forcing a vote.
Surface mental-model partiality
Each participant holds a partial-but-valid model; mental models are "resistant to change, especially among individuals who aren't personally experiencing any negative system effects".
Reframe a helpless team to 15% Solutions
LS 15% Solutions: locus-of-control reframe; *"Where do you have freedom to act? What's in your 15%?"* — without denying the 85%.
Apply What/So What/Now What sequence to the raw data
Three-question sequence imposes structure: What (data) → So What (pattern) → Now What (next step). Refuse jumping to Now-What.
Detect dominance pattern
FLO engagement-equity tracking, adapted as a contribution log; when one voice is dominating, pause and rebalance.
Use planning-poker-style estimates for retro vote weight
When voting on which retro item to deep-dive, private estimate → simultaneous reveal beats sequential reveal which anchors.
Team agrees too quickly
Until a decision is stated, honest disagreement is a duty; after it, everyone supports it as their own (Ch 3, "Professionalism"). Ask for the dissent before the vote.
Team is helpless ("nothing we can do")

Sort the deltas against MCDP 1's five examples of self-induced friction (unclear goal, lack of coordination, unclear or complicated plans, complex task organizations or command relationships, complicated technologies); the self-induced ones are the team's to act on (Ch 1, "Friction").
Surface doubt before agreement
Team agrees too quickly: groupthink symptoms (self-censorship, illusion of unanimity; adapted from Janis); write individually first and name a devil's advocate.

sections.section: Phase 3: Insight / cause analysis (the *why*, the system, the recurring pattern)
rows: Refuse the "root cause" framing
Cause-as-construction; *networked causality* replaces root cause; cause "is always something we create by recreating the event" (Appendix B) — scales down to retro level.
Refuse counterfactual reasoning
"If this person had done X..." is the forbidden move; learn why people did what they actually did, not what hindsight suggests.
Apply Five Whys with surprise-as-progress-signal
At a retrospective: ask "why" five times (give or take); "if you're rarely surprised by your root causes, you may not be digging deep enough."
Apply Five Whys from the Open Practice Library
OPL Five Whys practice: keep asking why until you find the real reason; when the answer is time, money or resources, ask why the process failed instead.
Test the recurring pattern against system archetypes
Five archetypes — Fixes that Fail, Success to the Successful, Shifting the Burden, Drifting Goals, Limits to Growth. Hypothesis-generators, not labels.
Build a CLD for the recurring problem
When the team needs a picture: causal loop diagram surfaces feedback loops producing the pattern.
Map mental models of the recurring problem
Each participant holds partial-but-valid model; surface partial models *before* discussing solutions.
Redirect blame language to system
*Action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate*; default-to-system prior surfaces in any retro where blame language is rising.
Re-read Norm Kerth's Prime Directive when blame surfaces
The Prime Directive is structural blameless-by-default commitment; especially important when blame language re-surfaces mid-retro.
Apply attribution-bias frame to participant accounts

Fundamental attribution error (underestimating situational causes, overestimating personal ones) pushes accounts toward individual blame; self-serving bias credits success to the team and failure to people outside the room (Ch 3.3). Redirect to conditions before individuals.
Apply confirmation-bias diagnostic

Confirmation bias "focuses on information that confirms existing beliefs" (Ch 7.3, Table 7.3): a team that has already decided what the problem is reads the board to confirm it; name the disconfirming sticky and ask the group to account for it.
Apply hindsight-bias diagnostic
Hindsight bias contaminating retro accounts; surface and bracket.
Detect a local fix for a systemic cause
"No single part of a system can ever bring overall improvement"; ask whether the insight points to a local symptom or a systemic pattern.
Detect drift on team norms / Definition of Done
Definition of Done is one of the five retro-inspection domains; if the DoD was not honoured during the Sprint, surface why as a process question, not a blame question.
Detect software-team measurement-driven framing

Goodhart's Law (measurement collapses under control pressure); cone-of-uncertainty as artefact; anchoring to a stakeholder's number; estimate peaks at multiples of seven hours (unit choice shifts the number).
Diagnose team dynamics stage (Tuckman) producing contested accounts
A storming team (members vying for leadership, choosing sides) may give contested data; read that as the stage, not pathology. Name the stage before treating the symptom.
Diagnose Five Dysfunctions pattern in insight phase

When artificial harmony (fast consensus, no disagreement) or a recurring problem shows up: test whether the chain (absence of trust → fear of conflict → lack of commitment → avoidance of accountability → inattention to results) explains it; naming the dysfunction locates the lever.
Name the ethical dimension of a recurring practice
When the retro surfaces a practice that harms someone outside the team (user, downstream colleague, customer), name it as an ethical gap — not just a process gap.
Check for safe-channel absence when problems went unreported
If a known problem was not surfaced in previous retros, ask what raising it would have cost and whether an internal channel existed (Ch 7.5).
Name the archetype mismatch precisely when recurring impediment is structural

"We are a CAPS-2 archetype ... being asked to deliver CAPS-3 outcomes ...; the cross-silo handoff that produces our recurring impediment is the structural mismatch, not a process problem." Precision beats vague "siloed" or "cross-functional issues" language.
Distinguish 15%-experimentable from structural-escalation

When team is naming structural impediments: which moves are genuinely within the team's locus of control (15% Solutions), and which would require changing the archetype itself — which the team cannot do unilaterally?
Detect the topology-mismatch pattern producing the recurring topic
Is this a Resource-drag pattern (utilisation pressure blocking end-to-end ownership)? A Delivery-bloat pattern (features unvalidated against outcome)? Name the pattern.
Apply local-optimisation test to proposed experiments

Before committing to multiple individually-defensible experiments, test: will they combine to improve the system goal, or will they compete? Primer: "If each element (e.g. policies, structures) is optimized in isolation, the performance of the whole system may actually decline."
Blame language surfacing

Critique rule: focus "not so much on the actions we took as on why we took those actions and why they brought the results they did" (Ch 3, "Training"). Pair with the NHS default-to-system prior and LFUO's counterfactual rule.
Name the kind of error behind a delta
A delta names a mistake: slip or lapse on a familiar task, rule applied in the wrong place, or no rule at all; "not paying attention" and "didn't follow the process" are not causes.
Reframe blame toward the setup
Blame language surfacing: ask "how did the organization fail the individual?"; if people expect errors to be punished, information about them stays obscure.
Name a normalised shortcut
Same pattern reappearing, or a shortcut defended because "it's always been fine": the bald-tire attitude; count the close calls.

sections.section: Phase 4: Experiment design (one or two owned experiments)
rows: Hold the one-or-two-experiments discipline
Field Guide: *"It's better to have one or two improvement items for the next Sprint than to have too much to change at once."* One or two changes at a time, not a list.
Limit the experiment list
Reduce the Batch Size practice: commit to the one or two experiments the team can finish; leave the rest on a visible backlog.
Split improvements into decisions vs actions
Decisions = changes to Definition of Done / Definition of Ready / Working Agreement; actions = new Backlog Items. Different mechanisms register different commitments.
Refuse adjournment without named owner
LS Discovery & Action Dialogues' closing question: *"Who will do what when next?"* — surfacing solutions and volunteers in one structure.
Resolve decision-rights ambiguity in experiment ownership
RACI matrix when ownership is ambiguous; the matrix is the artefact that registers the agreement.
Reduce batch size of the proposed experiment

"Reduce the Batch Size of your Efforts"; run the smallest version of the experiment that still tests the hypothesis; limiting WIP (here, concurrent experiments) is a consequence of batch-size reduction, not the other way around.
Refuse overwork commitments
Respect-for-people value pairs sustainable pace with Lean's Muri 無理; an exhausted team is "the perfect recipe for disaster".
Surface latent dissent before commit
Fist of five six-level voting before commit — *two or fewer fingers is the cue to stop, discuss and re-vote*; surfaces latent dissent the meeting tone is suppressing.
Frame the experiment as Design of Experiments
The hypothesis is named; the pass criterion is named; the measures and learning are named.
Refuse copy-without-principles
Establish Shared Principles practice; the experiment is grounded in the underlying principle, not just the surface practice.
Apply capacity-adjusted velocity discipline

When experiment will compete with delivery commitment for Sprint capacity: if carried-over work in process meets or exceeds forecast velocity and is all still valuable, *"we strongly recommend against taking in any new work this Sprint"* (Sprint Planning); commit only to experiments the team has real capacity for.
Apply Disagree and Commit when team is stuck
Against consensus-as-requirement; the experiment is committed to even if not unanimously endorsed; the disagreement is named, not buried.
Apply Locke goal-theory criteria to experiment design
Specific, stretching, accepted and committed-to (Locke) plus measurable and time-bound (SMART); vague experiments are non-commitments. Apply these criteria before adjourning.
Design for SDT autonomy — team chooses, not manager assigns
SDT: intrinsic motivation requires autonomy; assigned experiments produce lower follow-through than team-chosen ones. If an experiment must be assigned, build in modification latitude.
Choose the change model that fits the experiment scope
Lewin (stable, incremental), Kotter (urgency-framed, top-down), Cooperrider AI (abundance-based, bottom-up), CAS (self-organising). Match the model to the change's complexity and power distribution.
Name the ethical dimension before committing to an experiment
When the experiment crosses stakeholder boundaries — affecting users, customers, or colleagues outside the team — name it as an obligation (ethical minimum / maximum), not just an option.
Frame team-level experiments as topology-adjacent moves

Even within the existing archetype, what experiment moves the team rightward (broader skill mandate) or upward (broader work mandate) on the OT axes by a small amount? These are the genuine 15% moves available inside the current archetype.
Frame structural moves as escalation-with-evidence

If the insight is structural, the experiment isn't a team experiment — it's an escalation. Design it: who to, what evidence to attach (the OT mapping itself), what precise request (a structural experiment, not a permission or complaint).
Defend against framework-recommendation as retro experiment

"We should adopt SAFe / LeSS / Team Topologies" as a team-level retro experiment is the cargo-cult failure mode. Reframe: what topology do we need, and what concrete archetype change moves us toward it?
Use the Elevating-Kata-as-experiment framing for structural escalations

Structural escalations should propose experiments, not decisions: a defined small change with a named hypothesis, a check-point, and a re-mapping plan. This matches the retro experiment discipline (one or two owned experiments per retro).
Five experiments on the board
Main effort: recognise one action "as the most critical to success at that moment"; the others support it or wait (Ch 4, "Main effort"). Pairs with the Field Guide's one-or-two rule.
Give each experiment a purpose, not only a task
Commander's intent: "Of the two, the intent is predominant"; state the experiment as "[task] in order to [purpose]" so the owner can adapt when the task stops fitting (Ch 4, "Commander's intent").
Fit the experiment to the error type
The experiment is "be more careful", "double-check" or "train X": retraining a slip on a daily task is "a waste of time"; change the conditions that made the slip easy instead.
Add an experiment that limits harm
Every experiment makes a problem rarer: error reduction lowers frequency, only controls lower severity.
Close with What/So What/Now What
LS three-question sequence ending on Now-What with named next step; the closing structure when team needs a shape.
Apply the retro close: appreciations and meta-retrospective
Field Guide wrap-up: appreciations, then a few minutes retrospecting on the retrospective ("How did it go for the team? What would they like to try next time?").
Compress the take-away to six words
LS Six Words exercise — Mulago Foundation criteria (<8 words, verb, target population, measurable outcome); surface what's load-bearing.
Apply TC 25-20 closing-comments rule scaled down
Leader summarises key points, ends positively, links to next iteration, then leaves so team can discuss in private.
Reinforce modelling-as-through-line
The lead and coach model the practices they want the team to adopt, through the close: the lead models curiosity, the coach models transparent facilitation.
Mark experiment-not-done case for next-retro review

Capture each improvement where it will be seen: a Backlog Item for the next Sprint, or a change to the DoD, DoR or Working Agreement. Next retro's experiment review (Phase 0.5) names each one done or not done before new data.
Address closing-safety-check 1-2
Counsel-out discipline scales down: a participant who seems deeply struggling gets a private conversation after the retro, not a public prompt during it.
Confirm learning-as-precondition-for-improvement

"Learning is the key concept before continuous improvement can ever happen!"; Retrospectives are one of the source's named ways to run Learn and Improve Continuously; the experiment is downstream of learning, so confirm the team can say what it now understands that it didn't before.
File the retro output to the team's tracker (or markdown fallback)
Retrospective practice's outputs: action items / experiments to track; bound capability is `issue-tracker`, unbound is markdown.
Confirm the PDCA Act step is named before close
The retro is the Check step; Act must be named (owner, date, next Plan input) before the session closes. Unnamed Act = Check without consequence.
Cross-link to AAR axis when an event surfaces in retro
When the retro surfaces a specific incident the team wants to learn from in cross-functional shape, route to AAR.
Schedule the next OT re-mapping as a structural-check cadence

When structural escalation or archetype-mismatch work is in flight, close by naming when the team will re-MAP the archetype. Quarterly is defensible; tie it to a calendar date. "Periodic re-mapping with Org Topologies is an easy and fast way to complete a learning loop of feedback and adapting."
